# Measuring Crank and Rod Journals: A Practical Guide

Determining the runout and diameter of crankshaft journals is a critical step in engine rebuilding, but it presents unique challenges depending on how the block is cast. The specific scenario you describedâwhere main bearing caps are integral to the lower block rather than removable bolts-on piecesâfundamentally changes your measurement strategy. In traditional designs with separate caps, Plastigage is the standard diagnostic tool for clearance verification because it requires zero disassembly and provides an immediate visual readout of oil film thickness. However, when the caps are cast as one piece with the block, installing Plastigage becomes a logistical nightmare. You cannot remove the cap to check the bearing shell against the Plastigage strip without destroying the seal or compromising the casting interface. This forces you to rely entirely on micrometer measurements and bore gauges to infer clearance indirectly.

When dealing with integral caps, your workflow must shift from visual inspection to precise dimensional analysis. The primary metric to track is journal diameter, but accuracy here depends heavily on how you handle the crankshaft itself before it ever touches the engine block. Crankshafts are rarely perfectly round out of the box, often exhibiting ovality or taper due to manufacturing tolerances or previous grinding. If you measure the journal while the crank is resting freely on a workbench, the weight of the shaft will cause it to sag under its own mass. This deflection creates a false reading that does not reflect the actual geometry when the crank is supported by main bearings in the engine block. To get a valid measurement, you must support the crank at three points: one near each end and one in the middle. This triangulation prevents sagging and ensures the micrometer reads the true diameter rather than an artificially low number caused by elastic deformation.

Once the crank is properly supported, you measure the major axis (the widest point) and the minor axis (the narrowest point) at multiple intervals along each journal. The difference between these two readings gives you the total runout or ovality. For a production engine, tolerances are typically tight, often requiring less than 0.001 inch of variation per journal. If your major and minor axis readings differ by more than this threshold, the crankshaft has been distorted, likely from overheating or excessive load in a previous session, and may require grinding or replacement regardless of what the Plastigage would have shown.

Calculating the actual oil clearance requires you to factor in the bearing shell thickness and the block's bore dimensions. Since you cannot see the Plastigage strip, you must subtract the known ID of your new bearing shell from the measured crank journal diameter. If the resulting gap exceeds the manufacturer's specification, you have an overly large clearance that will lead to excessive oil pump-up and potential bearing failure. Conversely, a gap that is too small indicates a risk of seizure or overheating due to lack of lubrication.

In this specific setup where visual confirmation via Plastigage is impossible, the margin for error shrinks. You must ensure that your bearing shell installation is perfectly clean and seated before final assembly. Any debris left in the bore of an integral cap can alter the effective clearance by fractions of a thousandth of an inch. Additionally, verify that the main bearing journals are not out of round after any previous grinding operation. If the crank was ground to correct for wear in a previous rebuild, ensure the stock bearings you are using match the intended fitment class, as mismatched clearances can negate the benefits of the grind.

While this method feels more rigorous than Plastigage, it relies entirely on the precision of your measuring instruments and your ability to interpret the data correctly. There is no "look at the strip" moment to confirm a guess; every number you record must be accurate because there is no fallback visual check once the cap bolts down. This demands a disciplined approach to measurement and a deep understanding of the specific tolerances required for your engine's design.
